root.meaning: the place where coins are made; coin
root.note: The Roman mint was at the temple of Juno Moneta. What the name Moneta meant is disputed; the Romans linked it with monēre ‘to warn’, but that may be a later explanation.

stages.meaning: coins and notes you use to buy things

history: Money has its roots in ancient Rome. On the Capitoline Hill stood a temple of the goddess Juno Moneta, and near it the Romans made their coins. So monēta came to mean first ‘the place where coins are made’ and then ‘coins, money’. Through Old French moneie, the word reached English around 1300. English actually borrowed the same Latin word twice. Much earlier, Old English had taken monēta as mynet, ‘coin’, and that became mint, the place where coins are made today. What Moneta meant is not sure. The Romans themselves linked it with monēre, ‘to warn’, but this may be a later explanation.
historyEinfach: Money is a Latin word. In Rome, there was a temple of the goddess Juno Moneta. The Romans made their coins there. So monēta meant ‘the place for coins’, and then ‘money’. The word came to English through French. A mint is a place where coins are made. Mint is the same old word.

cognates.note: the same Latin word, borrowed much earlier

elsewhere.text: German Geld is a different word, but Münze, ‘coin’, comes from the same Latin monēta. Like English mint, it was borrowed very early.
In Spanish, moneda means a coin, and money is dinero. So Spanish kept the older meaning of the Latin word.

root.meaning: a name of Juno; her temple was the mint
